prompt: The picture numbers the three paths of travel in a lane. Which path is rider A using?
choices: Path 2, the center of the lane
Path 1, the left third of the lane
Path 3, the right third of the lane
The shoulder, outside the travel lane
explanation: Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle three paths of travel: path 1 is the left third, path 2 the center and path 3 the right third. Rider A is in path 1, the left tire track of cars, which many riders use as their default.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 15 (Lane Positions)

prompt: Using the path numbers in the picture: a car is beside you in the lane to your left and another is in the lane to your right. Which path is usually your best choice?
choices: Path 1, closer to the car on your left
Path 3, closer to the car on your right
Path 2, the center of the lane
Any path, as long as you ride faster than both cars
explanation: When vehicles are on both sides of you, the center of the lane, path 2, is usually your best option. It keeps the most space between you and both vehicles.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 15 (Lane Positions)

prompt: In the group shown in the picture, where does the leader (rider 1) ride?
choices: In the left side of the lane
In the center of the lane
In the right side of the lane
Beside rider 2, in the same row
explanation: In a staggered formation the group leader rides in the left side of the lane. The second rider stays at least one second back in the right side, and the third rider is in the left side at least two seconds behind the leader.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 38 (Staggered Formation)

prompt: The group in the picture comes to a series of curves. What should it do?
choices: Keep the staggered formation and close up the gaps
Move into single file through the curves
Ride two side by side so the group stays together
Spread across both lanes for more room
explanation: A staggered formation works on straight roads. It is best to move into single file when riding in curves, turning, and entering or leaving freeways or highways.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 38 (Staggered Formation)

prompt: Why does the formation in the picture place riders on alternating sides of the lane?
choices: It lets every rider use the center path in turn
It allows riders to talk while moving
It makes it easier for cars to pass between the riders in the group
It keeps the group close while each rider keeps a space cushion
explanation: The staggered formation keeps the ranks close and still lets each rider keep a safe distance from riders ahead, behind and to the sides. Never ride directly alongside another rider in the same lane.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 38 (Staggered Formation)

prompt: You are rider A. Oncoming car B is signaling a left turn across your path. What should you do?
choices: Keep your speed, since you have the right-of-way
Speed up so you clear the intersection before car B can start its turn
Slow down, cover the clutch and both brakes, and be ready to stop
Make eye contact with B's driver, then keep going
explanation: Cars turning left in front of you are one of the biggest dangers at intersections. Slow down, cover the clutch and both brakes to cut your reaction time, and be ready to stop. Having the right-of-way or eye contact does not protect you, because drivers often look right at a rider and still fail to see them.

prompt: Why is the situation in the picture so dangerous for rider A?
choices: Drivers turning left often fail to see an oncoming motorcycle
Motorcycles must yield to all turning vehicles
Car B has the right-of-way because it signaled before reaching the intersection
Motorcycles cannot stop as quickly as cars can
explanation: Over half of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by drivers violating a rider's right-of-way, and cars turning left in front of a rider are among the biggest dangers. Drivers often say they never saw the motorcycle.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 20, 22 (Intersections; Increasing Conspicuity)

prompt: Car B is passing rider A. Why is A's position in the center of the lane a good choice?
choices: It shows B that A is about to turn left
It keeps A clear of B's mirrors, wind blast and thrown objects
It makes room for B to share A's lane while passing
It lets A speed up and race car B to the next curve ahead
explanation: When being passed, stay in the center portion of your lane. Riding close to the passing vehicle risks a sideswipe, being hit by extended mirrors or objects thrown from windows, and wind blasts that can affect your control.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 16-17 (Being Passed)

prompt: As car B passes in the picture, what should rider A avoid?
choices: Staying in the center portion of the lane
Keeping a steady speed
Moving toward the passing car
Checking the mirrors
explanation: Riding close to the passing vehicle could put you in a hazardous situation. A slight mistake by you or the passing driver could cause a sideswipe, so keep a center-portion position and a steady speed.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 16-17 (Being Passed)

prompt: What is the problem with rider A's position in the picture?
choices: A is in car B's blind spot, so B may move over without seeing A
A is too far from the center line
A is following too far behind car B for the speed of traffic
A is riding in the wrong lane for passing the car ahead of it
explanation: One absolute rule of lane position is to avoid riding in another vehicle's blind spot. A driver changing lanes may never see a motorcycle beside the rear of the car.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 15, 18 (Lane Positions; Vehicles Alongside)

prompt: What should rider A do in the situation shown?
choices: Stay right beside car B so its driver can keep track of where you are
Honk and keep riding next to car B
Move to the far edge of the lane and hold that speed
Speed up or drop back so you are not alongside car B
explanation: Do not ride alongside cars or trucks in other lanes. You may be in a blind spot, and the vehicle blocks your escape route if you need it. Adjust your speed to get out of the blind spot.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 18 (Vehicles Alongside)

prompt: Rider A is passing a row of parked cars with no oncoming traffic. Why is A riding toward the left of the lane?
choices: To get ready for a left turn at the next corner
To make room for cars that want to pass on the right
To stay clear of opening doors and people stepping out between cars
Because riding close to parked cars is against the law in every state
explanation: When passing parked cars, stay toward the left of your lane. You avoid problems from doors opening, drivers getting out, or people stepping out from between cars. With oncoming traffic, the center of the lane is usually best.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 22 (Passing Parked Cars)

prompt: As rider A passes, one of the parked cars starts to pull away from the curb. What should A do?
choices: Speed up to get past before it moves out
Slow down or change lanes to make room for it
Hold your path; the driver must wait for you
Move to the right side of your lane to be seen
explanation: A driver pulling away from the curb may not check for traffic, or may look and still not see you, and cut into your path. Slow down or change lanes to make room for someone who might cut in.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 22 (Passing Parked Cars)
